text: This turkey is still frozen solid, and it's going into oil that's three hundred fifty degrees.
The ice on the skin flashes into steam the second it hits.
That part's not the problem. The problem is the ice deep inside the meat.
Raw turkey is mostly water, and as that ice melts, it drips out.
Water is heavier than oil, so it sinks straight to the bottom of the pot.
That's right over the flame, where the oil is hottest, and water boils at just two hundred twelve.
When water turns to steam, it takes up about seventeen hundred times more space.
So the steam blasts up through the oil and shoves it right over the edge.
The oil pours down the side of the pot, straight onto the burner.
One drop catches fire, and the flames race up the oil faster than it can fall.
In seconds, a fireball swallows the pot and climbs up the porch roof.
Turkey fryer fires kill about five people a year, and cause over fifteen million dollars in damage.
That's why you never fry a frozen turkey. Thaw it all the way, pat it dry, and keep the fryer far from the house.
